claims.text: Uber's engineering team decomposes total agent spend into six multiplicative terms: users, sessions per user, turns per session, requests per turn, tokens per request, and price per token.
Between February and mid-August 2026, Uber's weekly active users across agentic tools grew 7x and weekly agent requests grew 9.4x, while total AI spend stayed relatively flat from April onward.

Holding one model constant from February to July, Uber's cost per 1,000 model requests fell almost 34% from its peak and cost per session fell 52% from its June peak (self-reported, one company and one monorepo environment).

Uber nudges engineers in Slack at 50, 80, and 100% of expected spend, shows a live cost counter in each interactive tool's status line, uses one shared spend tier across interactive tools plus a separate tier for hosted fleet work, and requires manager approval for tier upgrades.

Uber's session-analysis dashboard flags 16 distinct anti-patterns, each paired with a financial impact and a remediation, including multi-turn sessions run on a frontier model when a smaller one would do.

Uber attributes more than 70% of its pull requests to local or cloud agents, and argues that optimizing a fleet of specialized managed agents with dedicated benchmarks is more cost-effective and scalable than optimizing individual terminal sessions.

Augment's recommended unit metric is spend per merged change: total fleet spend (provider consumption plus service fees) plus supervision hours costed at a loaded rate, divided by agent-attributed changes merged in the period; spend per completed task is used where no merge occurs.

Augment's budget model has three components: fleet spend (owned by the platform engineering lead), supervision hours (owned by the review/gate lead), and a platform ceiling of included allowance plus approved top-ups (owned by the VP Engineering with finance).

Augment bills usage at the provider's public API list price plus a flat 40% service fee on model inference with no fee on compute; the Standard plan is $20/month with $20 usage included and Business is $100/month with $100 included, both pooling up to 50 seats.
Augment's Cosmos routes each conversational turn to a model through Prism at 20 to 30% lower cost per task while preserving frontier quality.

Augment recommends against hard monthly token caps and token budgets for finance, preferring tiers, alerts before the ceiling, and manager sign-off, and warns that ranking engineers by token spend ('tokenmaxxing') rewards agent overhead.
Devin Enterprise bills in Agent Compute Units; Cognition flags sessions sized Large or Extra Large as unhealthy, starting above 10 ACUs on the standard scale and above 100 on the Enterprise scale.
GitHub prices its Copilot cloud agent at $0.01 per AI credit (set by model and tokens consumed) plus Actions minutes, while legacy annual Pro/Pro+ subscribers consume one premium request per session.
In an August 2025 internal survey, more than half of 132 Anthropic engineers and researchers said they can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of their work to Claude.
Anthropic reported that agents use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions and multi-agent systems about 15x more; early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries.

CloudZero's worked example (12 calls, 36,000 input and 6,000 output tokens per task) gives $0.132 per task on Claude Sonnet 5, $0.33 on Opus 5, $0.066 on Haiku 4.5, and $0.014 on GPT-5.6 Luna, i.e. $13,200 per month at 100,000 tasks on Sonnet 5.

In CloudZero's worked example, routing 8 of 12 steps from Sonnet 5 to Haiku 4.5 cuts task cost from $0.132 to about $0.088 (33%), and caching 2,000 of 3,000 input tokens per step cuts a Terra task from $0.144 to about $0.101 (30%).

Cache reads are priced near 10% of the input rate across the three major providers (5% on Anthropic's newest models), cache writes carry a 1.25x to 2x surcharge, and Google adds hourly storage rent; batch discounts of 50% apply to non-interactive agent tasks.

CloudZero found one Hudl employee driving $600K a year in token spend across 40 models, 70% of that company's total AI costs, unnoticed by finance and engineering; it recommends attributable API keys per agent and per-task token logging keyed to who triggered the run.
CloudZero recommends giving every agent a per-task budget and circuit breaker, so a runaway loop becomes a logged retry rather than an incident.

Splunk reports cached reads cost 10% of standard input price with break-even after about 1.4 reads of the same prefix, and that UC Berkeley's RouteLLM reported cost reductions up to 85% (85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, 35% on GSM8K) while keeping 95% of GPT-4 performance.
Splunk cites a workload running a frontier model at $200,000 a month that routed 60% of tasks to cheaper models and cut cost 42% with compliance intact.

Correlation One recommends step and tool-call budgets per task with explicit human escalation when exceeded, and recording token consumption per task as a test dimension, treating a correct workflow at 10x expected cost as a defect.

A 2026 study of eight frontier models on SWE-bench Verified found agentic coding tasks consumed roughly 1,000 times more tokens than code reasoning and chat, and a LeanOps audit of 30 engineering teams attributed 62% of the agent bill to re-sent context.
Per EY's 2026 analysis cited by Atlan, an LLM chat cost about $0.04 in 2023 versus about $1.20 per orchestrated agent workflow in 2026, roughly 30x higher.
